description: Nebula Forge is currently a three-person high school team in Chennai: Amudha Lakshmanan, Aadhav Vijay, Bhairavi Swaminathan. We know how to design the basis of the game, calculate the effects of trade-offs in space, and develop the website. We require team members proficient in graphic design and animation. If you think you would be a great value-add to the team please feel free to contact and reach out to us.
summary:
AP0GEIC 11 is a game where players design, launch and operate CubeSats. Every part affects the satellite's mass, power, data capacity, budget and mission duration, so players decide what matters most. Its 20 missions are based on real spaceflights, from Sputnik 1 to TROPICS. When a mission fails the game explains why and what happened in reality.

For the NASA challenge, we took the judges' idea of self-driving trucks and applied it to a space exploration problem: getting robots to navigate and dig safely near the Moon's south pole as part of Artemis. With the Sun barely 1–2 degrees above the horizon, long shadows can hide rocks across the Moon's surface, while some craters never receive sunlight. Players must choose sensors, find safe paths and decide when to move as shadows change, based on NASA research.

Space missions can fail for various reasons, from a satellite being too heavy for its rocket to a battery running out during an eclipse or software problems going unnoticed before launch. Most students never get the chance to make these decisions themselves. AP0GEIC 11 gives them that opportunity, letting them experiment, learn from mistakes and understand what real space missions can teach us.
details:
What it does and how it works

The game starts with four training puzzles, each introducing a different engineering concept. Players learn about mass by fitting a satellite into a rocket's payload slot, power by keeping it running through the dark part of every orbit, and data links by seeing how the slowest step affects transmission. The final puzzle introduces budgeting and scheduling, where players plan a mission year and deal with unexpected events along the way.

In the end 3 puzzles end with short animated videos showing what happens to the players design.

The game features 20 missions based on real spaceflights from the USA, USSR/Russia, China, India, Europe, Japan, the UK, Denmark and SpaceX. Each mission begins with a briefing, followed by a workshop where players build a 1U, 3U, 6U or larger satellite. They then test their design, launch it, manage it in orbit and receive a final report explaining what went right or wrong.

Event cards add a bit of pressure to the game, giving players just a short amount of time to make a decision. If they're unsure, they can use a free clue or pay for expert advice. After choosing, they find out whether their decision was optimal, fair or costly, along with an explanation of what it means for the mission. In nine missions, one of the options is actually what the real mission team chose, which players get to find out after making their decision.

The NASA challenge takes place through three rover puzzles near the Moon's south pole. Players first choose sensors such as cameras, stereo vision, lidar, radar, VIPER-style headlights and NASA Ames structured light before testing their rover. They then plan a safe route for a solar-powered scout rover around dust and shadows, and decide when it should move as the shadows change.

As players progress, earning stars unlocks new missions, with every seven missions forming a stage. They start with five lives, which refill over time, and can spend star dust to get extra lives. Answering 40 space trivia questions featuring NASA photographs also earns star dust. There is a logbook which keeps all the lessons in one place, alongside what happened during the actual missions.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Rather than simply reading about systems engineering, players get to experience it themselves. They see how changing one part of a satellite can affect its mass, power, data capacity, budget and mission duration. The game is free and runs in any web browser, so students, teachers, clubs and families can play without installing anything.

By including missions from different countries, we also wanted to show that space exploration is not limited to one nation. The NASA rover challenges introduce players to a current problem facing lunar exploration and let them explore it through decisions based on published research.

We have also included a Judge Demo Mode, which gives judges a five-minute guided tour with all features unlocked.

Tools and Technology

We built the game using Godot 4.7 and GDScript, with the Compatibility renderer so it could run as an HTML5 browser game. All the game content, including missions, satellite components, events, puzzles, trivia and rover routes, is stored in JSON files meaning we can add missions or change existing ones without having to rewrite the main code.

We also wrote automated tests to check the game rules, rover challenges, CubeSat sizing and mission unlocks. A separate solver checks that every mission can still be completed with three stars. The visuals and animations are our own work, while the trivia section uses public-domain NASA photographs. We use GitHub to share code and manage changes as a team, and GitHub Pages to host the game.

Creativity

We wanted each mission to bring a real spaceflight to life. Instead of just reading about what happened, players get to make their own choices, see how their designs turn out and compare their experience with what happened on the actual mission.

We also took the judges' self-driving truck idea and moved it to the Moon, where changing shadows and permanently dark craters make it much harder for robots to navigate safely.

We added smaller details to make the experience more enjoyable, including astronaut suits from different decades and countries, mission patch designs and celebratory animations when players earn stars.

Factors

Accuracy and Honesty - We used the CubeSat Design Specification Rev. 14.1 for satellite dimensions and mass limits. Mission histories are based on published information from NASA, ESA, ISRO and other sources, which are cited in the game. The lunar environment is based on NASA research into polar lighting, the IPEx excavator and VIPER's headlights. We distinguish measured figures from simulation assumptions: the approximately 97% structured-light detection rate comes from NASA Ames research, while prices, battery values and event effects are labelled as illustrative.

Accessibility - ince the game runs in a browser, players don't need to download or install anything. We kept the language simple, made sure text was readable and included hints for players who need help. Animations also play automatically without requiring no external input.

Learning curve - We wanted the game to be approachable even for someone with no prior knowledge of satellites. The four training puzzles introduce the basic concepts before players move on to full missions. The difficulty increases with each stage, and every failure is followed by an explanation so players can understand what went wrong.

Teamwork - We divided the work based on our individual responsibilities. Adity Agrawal and Tanvi Padala worked on art and animation, Anusha Chandra, Aadhav Dijay and Bhairavi Swaminathan handled software development, and Amudha Lakshmanan managed team coordination.
